page_contents_html:
Monoclonal Gammopathy of Undetermined Significance (MGUS)

MGUS is a premalignant plasma cell disorder characterised by a low-level paraprotein (M-protein) in the serum, without end-organ damage or haematological malignancy. It is not cancer.

Diagnostic criteria (all must be met)

  • Serum M-protein <30 g/L
  • Bone marrow clonal plasma cells <10%
  • No CRAB features (hypercalcaemia, renal impairment, anaemia, bone lesions)
  • No evidence of B-cell lymphoma or related disorder

Epidemiology

  • ~3% of people over 50; ~8.9% of people over 85
  • Progression risk: approximately 1% per year to myeloma, Waldenström’s macroglobulinaemia, AL amyloidosis, or lymphoma

Types of MGUS

  • Non-IgM MGUS (IgG, IgA, IgD): most common; may progress to multiple myeloma or AL amyloidosis
  • IgM MGUS: may progress to Waldenström’s macroglobulinaemia, AL amyloidosis, or lymphoma
  • Light chain MGUS: abnormal free light chain (FLC) ratio only; no intact M-protein detectable

Risk Stratification — Mayo Clinic / IMWG Model

Three independent risk factors for progression:

  1. M-spike ≥15 g/L
  2. Non-IgG paraprotein type (IgA, IgM, or IgD)
  3. Abnormal serum free light chain ratio (<0.26 or >1.65)
Risk factors presentRisk group20-year progression risk
0Low~5%
1Low-intermediate~21%
2Intermediate-high~37%
3High~58%

accordion_sections.heading: Primary care assessment
accordion_sections.html:
History

Ask about symptoms that could indicate progression to myeloma, AL amyloidosis, or Waldenström’s macroglobulinaemia:

  • Myeloma: bone pain (especially back and ribs), fatigue, recurrent bacterial infections, unexplained weight loss, thirst or polyuria (suggesting hypercalcaemia)
  • AL amyloidosis: ankle oedema, macroglossia, carpal tunnel syndrome, unexplained weight loss
  • IgM MGUS / Waldenström’s: visual disturbance, headache (hyperviscosity), peripheral neuropathy

⚠️ CRAB features — must not be missed

Any CRAB feature requires urgent haematology referral (USC / 2WW pathway).

FeatureThreshold
CalciumCorrected calcium >2.75 mmol/L
RenalCreatinine >177 μmol/L or eGFR <40 ml/min without other cause
AnaemiaHb <100 g/L without other cause
BoneLytic lesion, pathological fracture, or severe osteoporosis

Examination

  • Lymphadenopathy
  • Hepatosplenomegaly
  • Pallor
  • Bone tenderness
  • Peripheral oedema

Initial investigations at diagnosis

InvestigationPurpose
FBC, U&E, calcium, albumin, LDHBaseline / CRAB screen
Serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP)Identify and quantify paraprotein type and level in g/L
Serum free light chains (FLC)Kappa:lambda ratio for risk stratification
Urine Bence Jones proteinSpot urine protein:creatinine ratio; early-morning urine if raised
Skeletal surveyOnly if symptomatic — not routinely required for MGUS

Ongoing monitoring bloods

  • FBC
  • U&E
  • Calcium
  • Serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP) — to track paraprotein level over time

accordion_sections.heading: Primary care management
accordion_sections.html:
Monitoring intervals by risk group

Risk groupRisk factorsFirst checkSubsequent monitoring
Low0 RFSPEP + FBC/U&E/calcium at 6 monthsIf stable: annually for 2–3 years, then every 2–3 years
Low-intermediate1 RFSPEP + FBC/U&E/calcium at 6 monthsAnnually thereafter
Intermediate-high2 RFRefer to haematology — see ‘Who to refer’
High3 RFRefer to haematology — see ‘Who to refer’

⚠ Triggers to refer during primary care monitoring

Refer to haematology if any of the following occur during monitoring:

  • Paraprotein increase >25% from baseline AND absolute increase ≥5 g/L within 6 months
  • Any new CRAB feature (hypercalcaemia, renal impairment, anaemia, bone lesion)
  • New or worsening symptoms: bone pain, recurrent infections, unexplained anaemia, weight loss, hyperviscosity symptoms
  • Patient request for specialist review

Advice for patients

  • MGUS is not cancer
  • The vast majority of people with MGUS never develop myeloma
  • Monitoring is for early detection in the small proportion who do progress
  • Patients should report new symptoms promptly and not wait for their next scheduled review appointment

accordion_sections.heading: Who to refer
accordion_sections.html:
USC (2WW) / Same-day emergency haematology

  • Any CRAB feature (hypercalcaemia >2.75 mmol/L, creatinine >177 μmol/L or eGFR <40 without other cause, Hb <100 g/L without other cause, lytic bone lesion or pathological fracture)
  • Clinical suspicion of myeloma: significant bone pain, recurrent bacterial infections, hyperviscosity symptoms
  • Bence Jones proteinuria with raised urine protein:creatinine ratio

Urgent haematology (non-cancer pathway)

  • IgA or IgM paraprotein >10 g/L
  • IgG paraprotein >15 g/L
  • Paraprotein rise >25% within 6 months (minimum absolute increase 5 g/L)
  • Light chain MGUS (abnormal FLC ratio, no intact paraprotein detectable)
  • Diagnostic uncertainty

Routine haematology

  • 2–3 Mayo risk factors (intermediate-high or high risk group)
  • IgM MGUS of any level — consider discussion with haematology given Waldenström’s macroglobulinaemia risk
  • Patient request for specialist review

Include in all referrals

  • SPEP result: paraprotein type and level in g/L
  • Serum free light chain kappa:lambda ratio
  • FBC, U&E, LFTs, calcium, albumin
  • Urine Bence Jones protein result
  • Previous SPEP results where available (trend is clinically important)
  • Presence or absence of CRAB features
  • Current symptoms

accordion_sections.heading: Who not to refer
accordion_sections.html:
• Low risk MGUS (IgG paraprotein, M-spike <15 g/L, normal FLC ratio), asymptomatic and stable — primary care monitoring is appropriate
  • Very elderly or frail patients without symptoms — community monitoring is appropriate; if uncertain about management, discuss with haematology before referring
  • Patients not fit for or not wishing active treatment — community monitoring; email haematology for advice if unsure
  • Do not refer solely for an incidentally discovered low-level paraprotein — apply Mayo risk stratification first and refer only if criteria are met

notes_for_editor: No NICE CKS page exists for MGUS — NHS Scotland sources used throughout.
No D&G-specific local criteria document identified for MGUS — NHS Scotland regional guidelines applied.
IgM MGUS: even at low levels, recommend haematology discussion given Waldenström's risk. This is flagged in 'Who to refer'.
Light chain MGUS is classified as urgent (not routine) referral — ensure GP readers understand this subtype.
Skeletal survey is NOT routinely indicated for MGUS — only if symptomatic. Stated explicitly to prevent over-investigation.
